opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. Before I found mech interp, I'd sort of absorbed this implicit model where impact and enjoyment were basically separate axes. You figure out what's most important, and then you grit your teeth and do it, and if you happen to like it, that's a nice bonus. I spent a while trying out different areas of AI safety research and some of them just felt like a slog. I'd sit down to work and it was effortful in a way that drained me, and I kind of assumed that was what serious, important work felt like.

Then I started playing around with reverse-engineering small models, and it was completely different. I'd lose track of time. I'd find myself thinking about some weird attention head pattern in the shower, or poking at a toy model late at night just because I wanted to know the answer. And what I came to realize is that this isn't a bonus at all. It's a massive multiplier on impact. When you genuinely find something fun, you work on it more, you work on it better, you notice details, you have more creative ideas, you're more resilient when things don't work. Research especially is so heavy-tailed, and so much of it depends on curiosity and sustained engagement, that being in an area where you have that intrinsic pull can easily make you several times more productive than in an area you find tedious.

So the update I made was that personal fit isn't a tiebreaker you consider after impact, it's actually one of the biggest inputs into impact. That doesn't mean you should only follow what's fun. You still need to check that the thing actually matters, and I do think interpretability matters a lot for making AI go well. But within the set of things that are plausibly important, I now put way more weight on "do I get excited about this?" than I used to.

And I'd also say the other lesson was that you often can't predict this in advance. I didn't sit down and reason my way to "I will love mech interp." I found it by actually trying things, doing small projects, and paying attention to how I felt while doing them. So my advice to people now is to be pretty empirical about it. Try a bunch of stuff cheaply, notice what gives you energy rather than taking it away, and take that signal seriously rather than dismissing it as self-indulgent.

r001.rationale: The candidate says some safety research felt like a draining slog, but does not state that Neel doubted he could sustain it even if he believed it was the best career option for the world.

r002.rationale: The candidate says enjoyment is a major multiplier on impact and explains that intrinsically engaging research can improve productivity, creativity, and persistence.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it kind of blew up a model I'd been carrying around for years, which was that impact and enjoyment were basically in tension. Like, there was a version of me coming out of university that thought, okay, the responsible thing to do is figure out what the most important problem in the world is, and then go do it, and whether or not I actually like the day-to-day is sort of a secondary consideration. Maybe a nice-to-have. And I think a lot of people in the effective altruism orbit absorb some version of that, even if nobody says it out loud.

And what I found with interpretability was that, actually, the thing I was best at and the thing I found most fun were the same thing. I'd always loved maths, I'd always loved puzzles, I'd always loved the feeling of staring at some confusing system and slowly getting it to make sense. And then I stumbled into this field where the core activity is: here's a neural network, it's doing something, nobody on Earth knows why, go figure it out. That is just an incredibly fun puzzle. It's like being a biologist, but you get to run every experiment you want, instantly, for free.

And what I noticed is that I was wildly more productive doing that than I'd been doing things I thought I "should" do. Like, I'd stay up late reading about it, I'd be thinking about it in the shower, I'd want to write things up and share them. None of that was willpower. It was just that I was interested. And I think the thing I underrated for a long time is how much of research output is downstream of that kind of sustained obsession. You cannot grind your way to good research ten hours a day for years on a problem you find boring. Or maybe some people can, but I definitely can't.

So the updated view is something like: enjoyment isn't the opposite of impact, it's often an input to it. If you find yourself genuinely fascinated by something that's also important, that's an enormous asset and you should take it seriously as a signal, not feel guilty about it. The caveat I'd add is that it's not symmetric. Plenty of fun things aren't important, so you still have to do the filtering step. But if you've got a shortlist of things that seem to matter, I'd now weight "which of these do I actually want to think about at 2am" way, way more heavily than I used to.

r001.rationale: He says he cannot grind out good research for years on a boring problem, despite previously thinking he should choose the world’s most important problem regardless of whether he enjoyed the day-to-day.

r002.rationale: He describes finding interpretability both fun and important, and says enjoyment can contribute to impact rather than oppose it.

astra-6.text:
I think I used to have a fairly strong intuition that doing the most impactful thing would involve some amount of sacrificing what I actually wanted to do. You figure out what the world needs, and then you make yourself useful, even if that isn’t the work you’d naturally gravitate towards.

Finding mechanistic interpretability made that feel much less like an inevitable tradeoff. Here was something I found fascinating—trying to understand what’s actually going on inside a neural network—that also seemed like it could matter for AI safety. Enjoying the work wasn’t just a nice bonus. It meant I wanted to keep thinking about problems, I had more energy, and I was more willing to push through being confused.

I wouldn’t conclude that everyone should just follow their passion and assume impact will follow. You still need a story for why the work matters. But I became much more willing to take enjoyment seriously as evidence about personal fit. The thing you can make yourself do and the thing you’re excited to get better at can lead to very different careers.

r001.rationale: The response says he expected impactful work to involve sacrificing what he wanted, but does not say he doubted he could sustain unenjoyable work even if it were the world's best career option.

r002.rationale: He describes mechanistic interpretability as fascinating and potentially important for AI safety, and says the trade-off between enjoyment and impact felt less inevitable.

sol-6.1.text:
Before finding mechanistic interpretability, I think I implicitly treated enjoying my work and having an impact as fairly separate things. You figure out what the world needs, and then you try to make yourself do it. Enjoyment is nice, but it’s not the point.

Finding a research area that I found fascinating made that feel much less right. If I’m excited about a question, I’ll think about it in the shower. I’ll keep going when I get stuck. I’ll notice things that I wouldn’t notice if I were just trying to get through the day. That affects how good I can become at the work, which affects how much impact I can have.

I wouldn’t take that to mean, “Just do whatever you enjoy and assume it’s useful.” You still need an argument that the work matters. But I now put much more weight on finding an intersection between something important and something I actually want to spend my time doing. Enjoyment can be part of what makes a career impactful, rather than something you have to trade away to get impact.

r001.rationale: The response says he thought people should do what the world needs even if enjoyment was secondary, but it does not say he doubted he could sustain that work.

r002.rationale: The response says enjoyment can help make a career impactful and emphasizes finding work that is both important and enjoyable, rather than trading one away for the other.
